cricket_news.title: Bangladesh's spin gamble raises questions after Mirpur defeat
cricket_news.summary: News   •  West Indies tour of Bangladesh, 2026  Bangladesh's spin gamble raises questions after Mirpur defeat  With the West Indian spinners extracting more turn and out-bowling the hosts, it leaves Bangladesh with plenty to ponder over ahead of the Sylhet Test
cricket_news.content:
Did Bangladesh pay the price of preparing a spinning deck? It was a question that came up for discussion after the hosts’ eight-wicket loss to West Indies in the first Test at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium on Saturday (October 31).

While Bangladesh looked to take a significant step towards their dream of playing in the ICC World Test Championship final with a ploy of outfoxing West Indies with a spin-heavy attack, it hardly paid any dividends as the tourists emerged better placed for the strategy.

West Indies’ spinners dominated the Test, with left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican taking nine wickets, which included a five-wicket haul in the first innings. Captain Roston Chase took five wickets in the second innings with his off-spin to set up the match for his side before the batters got the job done.

The spinners from the two sides brought different bowling approaches. But what was more surprising was the fact that the West Indian spinners extracted a greater average turn - 3.5 degrees - compared to Bangladesh’s 3 degrees.

“I don't know why we have forgotten to turn the ball. If we cannot turn the ball on this wicket I am not sure where we will turn the ball,” a member of the national team management told Cricbuzz on the request of anonymity, after the Mirpur Test.

“I am not sure whether it is a technical thing or something else because these same bowlers managed to turn the ball better on flatter wickets.

“I think our bowlers tried to ball with more pace while the West Indians bowled a lot slower and that probably allowed them to turn the ball more than us,” he added.

There are also arguments over the Bangladesh spinners’ mindset and whether it presents them as attacking options.

“It's fair to say we are not traditionally attacking spinners as we believe that if we can stop the flow of the runs, pressure will mount on the opponents and most of our spinners play cricket carrying that philosophy," the aforementioned team management member said.

“We hardly have a plan B and you cannot ask them to change their approach right in the middle of the game. But the time has come for us to start having a plan B so that if needed, we can attack. And by that I mean having the courage to buy wickets.

“You can argue whether with such a small total [to defend] whether that would have been a good approach or not. But at the same time you cannot defend such a total with a mindset of not leaking runs,” he added.

Quite a few eyebrows were raised after Bangladesh opted for a spin-friendly wicket in Mirpur, considering that the strategy has resulted in more losses than wins in Tests in recent times. Moreover, Bangladesh’s fast bowlers have started to make a name for themselves through their recent performances and there is a feeling that not backing them to come good was not wise.

The absence of pace bowler Nahid Rana, who is ruled out of the series due to injury, would have played a part in making such a decision. But with the spinners unable to turn the ball as much as their opponents on a track tailor-made for them raises questions over the decision taken up by the team management.

Whether earning points in the WTC was a major reason behind this decision is a matter of discussion. But as they go back to the drawing board ahead of the second Test in Sylhet from November 5, Bangladesh have plenty to think about having endured successive defeats after their famous win against Australia in Darwin.

cricket_news.title: Jansen's long night of the soul dawns bright
cricket_news.summary: News   •  Australia tour of South Africa, 2026  Jansen's long night of the soul dawns bright  The South African allrounder capped a prolific series with a Player of the Series award after helping his side overturn a first-Test defeat
cricket_news.content:
Marco Jansen had one of those nights on Friday, a knotty, thorny sequence of long, dark hours when he goes “cuckoo in the head”, as he had told a press conference on Wednesday.

Back behind the microphones on Saturday, Jansen said: “I probably slept one-and-a-half hours, maybe two. That’s because of looking out my window, going to the bathroom, having a coke. I hardly got any sleep, thinking of what we could do, what I could do, what’s going to be required, what if things don’t go our way …”

Things did go South Africa’s way at Newlands on Saturday. Australia, who chased a target of 288, were bowled out for 111. That earned the home side the series 2-1 and put them on top of the ICC Test rankings for the first time since January 2016. It also hiked South Africa — the WTC champions — into second place in those standings. The Aussies, who started the series on top of the rankings and second in the standings, are now second and third. How did that feel?

“When we end up on the right side of things, for a split second there’s a sigh of relief that it’s over,” Jansen said. “But after that there’s a really good and excited and pumped feeling, knowing that if I played well I’ve contributed. And also if I didn’t play well I still contributed, whether it was on the field or off the field.

“This is a team thing. It’s not an individual thing, and that gives me a lot of joy and happiness. It makes it very much worth it.”

Jansen contributed directly in the first innings at Newlands, hitting seven fours in his 52 and taking 3/60 in the first innings. His second innings might have been what kept him awake on Friday night: he was bounced out by Mitchell Starc for an eight-ball duck. On Saturday he bowled eight wicketless overs for 17.

But he was named player of the series. That's what happens when you bring your team back into the rubber with a 100-ball 85 after they’ve slumped to 110/6. And then take 5/33. Jansen did that in the second Test at St George’s Park, where South Africa found a way to win by an innings and 31 runs after most of the first two days’ play was lost to rain and a wet outfield. And, on top of that, under the pressure of having lost the first Test at Kingsmead by 214 runs. Despite the size of those margins the series produced intensely competitive cricket.

“It wasn’t easy,” Jansen said. “There were a lot of ups and downs; ebbs and flows. It was never a case of one team having the upper hand for an extended period of time. There was a stage where I was sitting in the [Newlands] changeroom and you think, ‘Yes! We’re in this thing!’ And then four wickets fall and I’m like, ‘What the hell are we doing?!’”

Jansen’s exploits in the series have made him Test cricket’s top-ranked bowler and allrounder. Did that make him think of himself as special?

“No. I just see myself as a lightie [youngster] from Klerksdorp. When I started playing professionally and started my career for the Proteas I never thought of getting into the top 10 bowling or allrounder rankings. Fast forward to now where I’m on top of those lists; firstly it’s surreal and secondly, like my dad used to tell myself and my brother [Duan], ‘Moenie dat jou kop te groot raak nie [don’t let you head get too big]. I remind myself where I come from and what I’ve had to be to be consistent and perform consistently.”

Maybe Jansen’s most valuable asset is that he has maintained the link between his smalltown former life and the big time he has reached.

“How old am I now? Twenty-six? [Correct]. Eight years ago I was in high school, and I was watching these guys on TV doing their thing. Now I’m in Cape Town, where a lot of people are watching us.

“I’m better prepared mentally if things don’t go our way, or if we’re doing well, or if I’m batting or bowling well, to stay calm and composed. To handle those situations better is the difference.”

Jansen can afford to be more inwardly focused than Temba Bavuma, who has to answer not only for himself but also for the team he captains. Happily for all concerned Bavuma is good at that.

“In a weird way, but also a beautiful way, we are driven by this ambition to achieve what it is that we want to achieve; the narratives and the sentiments and the stories that are created around it all,” Bavuma told a press conference.

“You have to answer questions why a certain guy is playing. But we stick to what we want to achieve, and we’ve surpassed a lot of those things. Did I think two or two-and-a-half years ago that we’d be in this position? Probably not.”

Key to that happening is Shukri Conrad, South Africa’s imaginative, maverick coach. How he and Bavuma, who comes across as measured and logical, get along is a fascinating study in contrasts. But, clearly, they do.

“Shuks uses a crazy formula. I keep questioning him to make sure we’re making the right decision. But, whatever decision we make, we back it with 100% conviction.”

Bavuma called the series, in which all three matches went to five days, “an enthralling 15 days of cricket”. He also labelled it “15 days of pressure”.

Now that the pressure’s off here’s hoping Bavuma, and Jansen, sleep well on Saturday.

cricket_news.title: Zaman, Minhas and Baig power Pakistan's tri-series triumph
cricket_news.summary: Reports   •  ODI tri-series, 2026   Zaman, Minhas and Baig power Pakistan's tri-series triumph  The Pakistan trio trumped Kamindu Mendis' century as they chased down Sri Lanka's 325/8 with three wickets to spare
cricket_news.content:
Fakhar Zaman's century trumped Kamindu Mendis' ton as Pakistan secured a three-wicket win in the final against Sri Lanka in Lahore to clinch the tri-series. Mendis' 131 and Pavan Rathnayake's 77 were instrumental in Sri Lanka posting 325 for 8. Pakistan's chase was powered by Zaman's 127, along with important contributions from Saad Baig (74) and Arafat Minhas (31-ball 61) as the hosts overhauled the target with 1.3 overs to spare.

Sri Lanka made a steady start after being asked to bat, with Avishka Fernando and Kamindu Mendis negotiating the new ball before gradually shifting gears. Fernando struck two fours and a six off Naseem Shah in the sixth over to inject some momentum while Kamindu hit a maximum off Shaheen Afridi in the 10th over, taking Sri Lanka to 51 for 0. Kamindu was given out caught behind off Arafat Minhas but successfully overturned the decision on review. Pakistan, meanwhile, bowled some tight overs, including a maiden from Haris Rauf to Fernando in the 17th, before Salman Agha capitalised in the next, trapping Fernando lbw for 38.

Kamindu ended a boundary drought and went past fifty while Kusal Mendis launched Rauf for a six. But Agha produced a moment of brilliance to dismiss Kusal, taking a sharp return catch to leave Sri Lanka at 109/2 in the 22nd over. Pakistan had an opportunity to put the brakes on the innings, but Kamindu and Pavan Rathnayake ensured Sri Lanka made good progress. The pair put on a century stand, the scoring rate picked up, and milestones followed as Kamindu reached his maiden ODI century while Rathnayake brought up his fourth 50-plus score in the series, taking Sri Lanka past 250 in the 41st over.

The third-wicket pair added 146 before the partnership ended when Kamindu was trapped lbw by Afridi. Dasun Shanaka smashed a six and two fours in a quickfire 17 off nine balls before Afridi dismissed him, while Rauf accounted for Rathnayake and Naseem sent Janith Liyanage back, as Sri Lanka lost five wickets for just 29 runs. However, Sahan Arachchige and Maheesh Theekshana added some useful runs towards the end to help Sri Lanka set a challenging target for Pakistan.

Pakistan's chase began with a couple of setbacks as Dilshan Madushanka bagged the wickets of Maaz Sadaqat and Babar Azam in his first two overs. Fakhar Zaman and Saad Baig ensured that the innings did not stagnate in their bid to consolidate. Zaman struck maximums wile Baig dealt in regular boundaries, taking Pakistan to 50 for 2 after 10 overs. The pair maintained a steady scoring rate, with Baig bringing up his maiden ODI fifty and Zaman crossing fifty as well, with the century partnership sandwiched between the milestones.

Pakistan crossed 150 in the 26th over before the 149-run third wicket stand came to an end when Baig handed a catch back to Theekshana to depart for 74 off 75, with 11 fours in his outing. Zaman, meanwhile, continued unperturbed as he brought up his 12th ODI hundred and cleared the fence regularly. He was eventually bowled by Madushanka, with his 99-ball knock including six sixes and 11 fours. Salman Agha followed a short while later, bowled by Dunith Wellalage, leaving Pakistan needing 96 off the last 13 overs, which became 82 off the last 10 overs.

Pakistan went through a dry spell, without any boundary, for 10 overs before Arafat Minhas struck a four off Shanaka in the 43rd over, and another boundary off Asitha Fernando in the 45th. Hasan Nawaz's scoring was on the slower side but he supported Minhas in building a partnership as they brought the equation to 46 off the last five overs. A couple of good overs for Pakistan, which included sixes for Minhas off Shanaka and Madushanka, made it 18 off 18. Minhas brought up a 28-ball fifty with a six off Fernando, followed by another maximum and a four before he was eventually dismissed. Faheem Ashraf fell in the same over but Pakistan got over the line when Afridi struck a six off Madushanka in the penultimate over.

Brief scores: Sri Lanka 325/8 in 50 overs (Kamindu Mendis 131, Pavan Rathnayake 77; Shaheen Afridi 2-50) lost to Pakistan 331/7 in 48.3 overs (Fakhar Zaman 127, Saad Baig 74, Arafat Minhas 61; Dilshan Madushanka 3-63) by 3 wickets.

cricket_news.title: Rabada, Harmer bowl South Africa to series win and No. 1 ranking
cricket_news.summary: Reports   •  Australia tour of South Africa, 2026  Rabada, Harmer bowl South Africa to series win and No. 1 ranking  Australia, chasing 288, were bowled out for 111 to give South Africa a 176-run win in the third Test in Cape Town
cricket_news.content:
All three results were possible when the final day of the series began at Newlands. By Lunch, only one result was on the table. Kagiso Rabada struck twice in the first over and Simon Harmer spun a web with figures of 6 for 16 as Australia, chasing 288, were bowled out for 111 to give South Africa a 176-run win in the third Test. As a result, the hosts also took the series 2-1 and reclaimed the No. 1 Test ranking.

Australia must have begun the day believing they could chase this down. That belief, though, lasted three balls. Rabada, who was down with illness on the second and third days, had Matt Renshaw, the series' leading run-scorer, gloving a ball down the leg side to Ryan Rickelton. Three balls later in the same opening over, he trapped Marnus Labuschagne lbw.

Travis Head, Australia's best hope, hit three fours before Rabada had him caught at gully by Marco Jansen in the seventh over. It was Rabada's 350th Test wicket, and Australia were reeling at 22 for 3 at the time.

Harmer came on in the 12th over and found sharp turn out of the rough straight away. To make things worse, Josh Inglis was run out for four after a needless single to silly point. In the 18th over, Harmer had Alex Carey caught off a reverse sweep, with Marco Jansen diving forward at backward point. Two balls later, Cooper Connolly was caught behind. Mitchell Starc survived 24 balls before popping a catch to short leg off the last ball of the morning session and Australia went to Lunch at 60/7, having lost seven wickets in the morning.

Cameron Green and Pat Cummins then dug in, with 11 successive overs gone without a run. Green, on 27 off 110 balls, finally tried to break the shackles, dancing down to Harmer, and was bowled through the gate. Cummins batted 90 balls for 11 and added 45 for the ninth wicket with Nathan Lyon, who made an unbeaten 33, before Harmer trapped him lbw. Two overs later, Harmer bowled Josh Hazlewood with a ball that drifted in and turned away to hit the top of off, bowling Australia out for 111 in 57.1 overs and bringing up a famous series win for South Africa.

Harmer, who took 21.1 overs to claim his six wickets, 14 of them maidens, became the first South African spinner to take a Test ten-wicket haul at Cape Town. Rabada, who had set off this slide with the new ball, finished with 3 for 39.

The win was set up on the fourth day by Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder, whose centuries and 154-run sixth-wicket stand pulled South Africa out of trouble and gave them a total to defend.

It was Australia's first Test series defeat since March 2023, and only the fourth time they have lost a three-match series after winning the first Test. As a result of them going down, New Zealand claimed the first position on the World Test Championship table, pushing Australia out of the top two for the first time this cycle.

Brief scores: South Africa 329 (Marques Ackerman 95, Marco Jansen 52; Mitchell Starc 6-72) & 387 (Wiaan Mulder 115, Ryan Rickelton 101; Mitchell Starc 3-65) beat Australia 429 (Josh Inglis 102, Alex Carey 80; Simon Harmer 4-104, Marco Jansen 3-60) & 111 (Nathan Lyon 33*; Simon Harmer 6-16, Kagiso Rabada 3-39) by 176 runs.

cricket_news.title: 'We came here to win the series': Chase keeps West Indies focused
cricket_news.summary: News   •  Dhaka Test  'We came here to win the series': Chase keeps West Indies focused  West Indies are looking to seal a series win in Sylhet after taking an early lead in Dhaka, while Bangladesh's hopes of reaching the WTC final have suffered a major setback
cricket_news.content:
West Indies captain Roston Chase said on Saturday that they are eyeing a series win over Bangladesh to end the current ICC World Test Championship (WTC) cycle on a high.

West Indies earned an eight-wicket win over Bangladesh in the opening Test of the two-match series in Dhaka, which is part of the ongoing WTC cycle.

Both teams will now move to Sylhet for the second Test, scheduled to begin on November 5.

The touring skipper said they were not getting carried away after winning the series opener, as the job was still only half done.

"Winning a Test match anywhere in any conditions is a beautiful feeling, but we came here to win the series. This is just the first of two legs," said Chase.

Chase said the bowlers broke the backbone of Bangladesh's batting in the second innings by picking up quick wickets, which set the tone for them in the game.

"I think the start that we had in the second innings with the ball, I thought that we put them under pressure and we got, I think it was four quick wickets early in that second innings," Chase said.

"I thought that really broke the back of the Bangladeshi batting and then we just had to stay patient from there and try to get the other wickets, and that we did.

"I don't want to say we let them off, but I thought especially Nayeem this morning played well for the 50 that he got and he kept us out there longer than we wanted to be. But as I said, we stayed patient and we stuck to our plans and our processes and we got them to a total that we thought was more than manageable," he added.

"I thought 170 was manageable because I thought the wicket was still a good wicket. I didn't think the wicket had any devils in it, it was still playing consistently. I thought it had a bit of bounce as well, probably the first time I saw a wicket in Dhaka with so much bounce," he said.

"I just wanted us to go out there and get a good start and I thought that was the key, and that we did. And then I just wanted my guys to go out there and play with intent. Although Bangladesh have some good spinners and whatnot, I just wanted them to go out there and, if the Bangladeshi spinners are offline, try to punish them," he said.

"Don't let them just settle and bowl and bowl and bowl, because we know when they get into that rhythm and they start spotting the ball in front of you and they start to get that confidence, and then things start to happen. So I just thought that start was very key for us as well," he added.

Chase said they had taken a last-minute decision to leave out Kemar Roach and play spinner Joshua Bishop after the pitch was shaved on the first morning.

"It was shocking for us to see that much grass off," Chase said. "We made a last-minute change in leaving out Roach and bringing in Bishop."

"When the green grass got shaven off, I thought it would be more suitable for the spinners. I thought that we read it correctly," he added.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto said their dream of reaching the World Test Championship final had become difficult after the defeat to West Indies.

A win against West Indies would have put them in a strong position towards their goal of earning a spot in the WTC final, but the defeat has dented their hopes. They now need four wins and a draw from their remaining five Test matches against West Indies, South Africa and England.

"It's difficult, to be very honest. But as I said in the first press conference, we are looking at one match at a time. This Test match we didn't play our best. So looking forward to the second Test, how we come back strongly," said Najmul, while rejecting suggestions that the points table had influenced the preparation of the surface.

"The points table did not come to mind. The condition was set by thinking about the opponent's strengths and weaknesses. I don't think it was made thinking about the Test Championship final," he said.

"Spinners have always won us matches in the past. That confidence was there before and it is still there. I don't think we made too many mistakes about the conditions," he said.

"After setting 170, we believed it could be defended, given the state of the pitch. Unfortunately, that didn't happen. We could have bowled a bit better on this wicket. We didn't bowl very well," he said.

"We could not pick the length very well. It was a bit scattered. In the fourth innings we took only two wickets," he added.

Najmul pointed to his own first-innings batting as a key factor in the defeat, saying he should have taken greater responsibility as a senior batter.

"In the first innings, I should have taken more responsibility as a senior batsman. I have played here for a long time and I know these conditions. If I could have made a big score, the team could have been 370 instead of 270," said Najmul.

"We fell back in the first innings. We knew batting later would be difficult. I would say the mistake was made in the first innings," he said, adding that they also missed Mushfiqur Rahim, who sat out the Test after injuring his finger during preparations for the opening game.

"We missed him. An experienced cricketer in this kind of condition. It would have been good if he was here," Najmul concluded.

cricket_news.title: Yuvraj Singh sees a leader and an ODI batter in Abhishek Sharma
cricket_news.summary: News   •  India cricket  Yuvraj Singh sees a leader and an ODI batter in Abhishek Sharma  The India legend, who introduced Abhishek to golf, believes the opener has the leadership qualities to take on greater responsibility and deserves a place in the ODI squad
cricket_news.content:
Whether golf can really help a cricketer's batting skills is a matter of interpretation, particularly because the ball is stationary in the game of greens and fairways, while it is necessarily in motion in the game of bat and ball. That said, cricketers are known to possess the hand-eye coordination that golf also demands, and the sport could further augment that skill, apart from helping in swing movement, power-hitting, ball sense and competitive drive. Abhishek Sharma may be a classic example.

Cricketers are known to take to golf like a fish to water, more so overseas players than Indians, but Abhishek has already developed a liking for the sport. He is often spotted on the fairways with his guru, Yuvraj Singh, who, it is said, introduced his disciple to the game during the Covid pandemic. Abhishek has since taken to golf seriously and is often seen at golf courses of Chandigarh and New Delhi with Yuvraj.

Both also strolled on the green expanses even in exotic cities and locations. Earlier this summer, they went to play a few rounds during visits to Sardinia, an island in Italy, and Marrakech, in Morocco, before that. So taken is Abhishek with swinging his club around that he would even play the golf regularly during the IPL, joining his overseas teammates, who rarely miss an opportunity to hit the course, whether in Hyderabad or at other IPL venues where SRH play their away games.

His golfing skills may well be reflected in his batting — in his huge bat swing, power-hitting and timing. With experience, he is also committing fewer mistakes and often gets the ball to attain both altitude and distance, a skill that golfers often seek to develop through the swing of the club: both height and distance.

“Golf helps with the bat swing and head position a lot. The top hand, which in Abhishek’s case is the left, gets extended, and that helps with the swing. It also helps with temperament. In golf, you tend to make mistakes, but you also learn to make course corrections. So it can help minimise mistakes and build concentration, which should come in handy in cricket too,” says Kiran More, a habitual golfer, explaining how the sport could be helping Abhishek.

“I have introduced him to golf so that he can unwind from cricket,” says Yuvraj Singh, an avid golfer himself, of course. But Yuvraj, who was in Mumbai for a promotional event on Friday, addressed the two elephants in the room — when and whether Abhishek would be ready for the ODIs and whether he was prepared to take on a leadership role.

Abhishek is being particularly credited with mentoring Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the teenager who is yet to cement his place in the national side despite his abundance of talent. The chemistry between Abhishek and Sooryavanshi, on display during the third T20I against New Zealand in Wellington recently, made for a pleasing sight.

The two put on 133 for the first wicket in 7.1 overs with Abhishek hammering a breathtaking century and Sooryavanshi hammering a typically belligerent 45 off 19 balls. There was no sign of insecurity in Abhishek in the way he treated and encouraged Sooryavanshi. On another occasion, it was Abhishek, who was first to comfort Sooryavanshi after he had missed a century (97 off 29 balls) in the IPL Eliminator earlier this year even though his own franchise was at the receiving end of his sensational batting.

“Well, it’s too early to say whether he has the makings of a captain, but I feel he has all the qualities of a leader. I think he encourages the younger guys in state cricket as well. I love the way he encourages Sooryavanshi, puts his hand on his shoulder and motivates him. I think that’s a good sign of a senior leader, whatever you want to call it,” Yuvraj tells Cricbuzz.

“If you want to captain India one day, I think it’s important to captain your IPL side. That gives you the kind of confidence you need to lead India. I’m sure time will tell whether he is capable of doing it. If it’s in his destiny, I’m sure he’ll get the opportunity. If not, then so be it. But I’m sure he’ll finish as a great white-ball player, whether he becomes captain or not.”

Yuvraj also called for Abhishek’s inclusion in the ODI set-up, something one understands, even India head coach Gautam Gambhir wants. “Whether he has scored 35, 100 or 31, 100, the point is that he has been performing consistently in white-ball cricket for a very long time. What more he needs to do to get into the ODI squad, I don't know. Maybe he needs to contribute more with his bowling and fielding. But that will only happen if he gets an opportunity to play.

“There are always areas to improve, and I think unless you give a player a chance, where is he going to showcase his talent? I understand that the situation is difficult right now because there is so much competition for places in the squad, along with some big names. But look at Sooryavanshi. He was brilliant and made his own place in the T20 squad. If you feel that Abhishek is performing brilliantly at the moment, then somewhere you have to make a place for him to play 50-over cricket until the World Cup.”

cricket_news.title: India seek bowling solutions in bid for 4-1 finish
cricket_news.summary: Previews   •  India tour of New Zealand, 2026  India seek bowling solutions in bid for 4-1 finish  India have secured the series but their bowling numbers since the T20 World Cup remain a concern heading into the final game against a resurgent New Zealand
cricket_news.content:
No time to rest. With just one intervening day before the switch from Eden Park to Seddon Park, the final T20I of the series (and India’s 40th of the year) turns into a short stopover. The attention has already started drifting towards the one-dayers, especially since India’s decorated batting duo has landed on the same island for the 50-over challenge.

India have pocketed the T20I series, but the manner of their 87-run defeat in Auckland was a reminder that New Zealand haven’t exactly been blanked out, but outmuscled in a series deep-fried in runs.

Shreyas Iyer called the defeat a “great learning curve,” conceding that Eden Park’s unique dimensions posed a fresh challenge for many within the team. The home team fared better on the ground with a short straight boundary, extra bounce, and strong winds that prevented dew, powering to 259 and handing India their second-heaviest run-defeat ever.

India wouldn’t have minded the hiccup: the series has allowed them to test out combinations, move things around slightly, and find new batting heroes. But the bowling, particularly in the second half, has been a cause of worry. Among Full-Member sides, India have the worst average and second-worst economy since the T20 World Cup this year.

New Zealand have been served greatly by an in-form Glenn Phillips, who has been exceptional at shifting gears, and found support in Daryl Mitchell, Bevon Jacobs and Michael Bracewell. Mitchell Santner has been the standout bowler across both teams, while Jacob Duffy came back strongly after leaking runs in two games. They’ve managed to put India’s batting under pressure twice, and it came by restricting them in the Powerplay. That could be the defining factor in the final game as well. As could be their catching: New Zealand have dropped as many as 12 this series.

When: India vs New Zealand, 5th T20I, November 1, 2026, 12:30 PM IST, 8:00 PM Local time

What to expect: Compared to Auckland, it gets cooler in Hamilton, with temperatures dropping to as low as 4 °C early morning. It’s likely to hover between 12-15 °C during match times. The winds, though, might not be as big a factor. Seddon Park has usually been a high-scoring venue, and the run-fest is likely to continue.

New Zealand: The hosts have changed around their pace attack as well, some of which have been forced. Lockie Ferguson and Matt Henry are injured, and Kyle Jamieson will re-link with them in the ODIs. It’s given a surprise chance to Matthew Fisher, and the quick has taken three wickets in his two appearances so far. Now that they’ve broken the losing streak, they might consider sticking with the same combination.

Predicted XI: Tim Seifert (wk), Finn Allen, Daryl Mitchell, Glenn Phillips, Bevon Jacobs, Michael Bracewell, Mitchell Santner (c), Nathan Smith, Adam Milne, Jacob Duffy, Matthew Fisher

India: Ishan Kishan, who had been ruled out of the second and third T20I, returned in the fourth, also taking up wicketkeeping duties. It remains to be seen whether Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, swapped in and out for those two games, gets a chance in the dead rubber, especially if Sanju Samson isn’t taking the gloves.

A pace-heavy lineup hasn’t afforded space for Kuldeep Yadav and Varun Chakaravarthy yet, despite Axar Patel’s poor returns. All four quicks have been given sufficient game time around Arshdeep Singh’s fixed spot. They could go back to Bhuvneshwar Kumar, whose much-awaited comeback has produced only one wicket in three games.

Predicted XI: Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson/Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Ishan Kishan (wk), Shreyas Iyer (c), Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Nitish Kumar Reddy/Shivam Dube, Naman Dhir, Arshdeep Singh, Prince Yadav/Bhuvneshwar Kumar, Mayank Yadav

- India have conceded 200+ 11 times in 39 matches, the most by a team in a calendar year across all T20 cricket

- Glenn Phillips now has more runs (276) than anyone against India in a T20I series

- New Zealand’s catching success this year stands at 74.1 per cent, the second-worst among the top-12 ranked T20I teams in the world, after Pakistan (73.1)

"You need a ton of runs to even have a sniff of beating India, so for us to be able to put that sort of score on the board today (259), I guess it'll give us confidence going forward. It's our first time being up in that 250 range, at least in the time that I can remember. I don't think you've ever got enough to feel comfortable with this side." – New Zealand batter Glenn Phillips after the 4th T20I.

“Some phenomenal shots, which were like pure bliss. Kudos to him. He's been consistent throughout the series, so a lot to learn from him,” India captain Shreyas Iyer, on Phillips’s knock in the 4th T20I.

cricket_news.title: Daylight at last between South Africa and Australia
cricket_news.summary: Match Features   •  Australia tour of South Africa, 2026  Daylight at last between South Africa and Australia  Rabada set the tone with a devastating opening burst before Harmer ran through the lower order, completing a memorable series win for the hosts
cricket_news.content:
Three balls of the morning session remained at Newlands on Friday when Wiaan Mulder backed away from the stumps with Mitchell Starc well into his magnificent impression of a swan swooping towards the bowling crease.

Starc slowed, stopped, turned around, went back to his mark, and started off again. Again Mulder held up a hand and retreated, this time because Starc’s towel had escaped his waistband and landed on his run-up, clearly in the batter’s eyeline.

Starc went back from whence he had come, but as he passed the stumps he paused to switch the bails. Just for laughs.

Ryan Rickelton, the non-striker, was having none of that. Once Starc was safely in the outfield, his back turned to the stumps, Rickelton returned the bails to their original position.

That he did so without removing a batting glove was impressive in its own small way. Because, when you’re wearing batting gloves, just about all your hands are able to do is hold a bat. Almost everything else is like trying to get a carrot into a keyhole.

For the first 14 days of this gripping series that kind of detail was seized on in an effort to put a sliver of daylight between the teams. Because there is so vanishingly little to separate them. Skilled, resourceful batters? Quality quicks? Canny spinners? Bristling fielding? Feistiness? Both sides tick all of those boxes.

Thus it jarred when Australia won by 214 runs at Kingsmead and South Africa by an innings and 31 runs at St George’s Park. Were these teams really that good? Yes. They needed to be to emerge from complex situations to earn victories, nevermind by those margins. These teams really were that good, hence them being beaten so emphatically was shocking.

Saturday, the 15th day of the series, was also shocking. But not in the same sense. Kagiso Rabada strangled Matt Renshaw and trapped Marnus Labuschagne, who offered no stroke, in front in the first over of Australia’s search of 288 to win. In the seventh Rabada completed his domination of the top order by inducing a wild drive from Travis Head that took the edge and flew to gully, where Marco Jansen took the catch to reduce the Aussies to 22/3.

Good players take advantage of favourable situations to bend the game in their favour. Great players create those situations. Rabada showed, not for the first time, that he is among the latter. And he was duly rewarded — Head was his 350th Test wicket, and he took it with his 13,808th delivery. That is comfortably the fastest in the history of the game by any bowler from any country. Dale Steyn, who is next on the list, needed 911 more balls to reach the milestone.

Australia shambled to 60/7 at lunch, losing Cameron Green to a runout and Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly and Starc in the last 37 deliveries of the session. The last three tumbled to Simon Harmer, who bowled with urgent aggression and found zagging turn to claim those wickets in 29 deliveries without conceding a single run.

Harmer’s startling economy was partly of his own making, but also due to the Aussies’ lack of attacking sensibility. Green shared stands of 17 off 36, 18 off 51, two off 11 and 18 off 50. Many runs were refused, and that was even before Pat Cummins took guard. Rabada has dismissed Australia’s captain seven times in 10 Tests, and so the plan was to protect Cummins from South Africa’s ace.

Green and Cummins had amassed a painstaking two off 73 balls when Temba Bavuma found a novel way to put an end to the silliness. Harmer bowled all of his 13 overs from the Wynberg End. For his 14th he was switched to the Kelvin Grove End to train his sights on Green — who lurched down the pitch to the first delivery and was bowled through the gate.

At 62/8 less than an hour after lunch Australia were on their way to the abattoir. Then they went into hibernation. Cummins and Nathan Lyon had eked out 45 off 104 when tea loomed. Along with Harmer. Cummins played for turn. There wasn’t any, and he was hit on just enough of his back thigh to be leg-before.

Tea was promptly postponed. A good thing too. Ten deliveries later — six of them bowled by Aiden Markram — Harmer fizzed one past Josh Hazlewood’s bat and through the top of his off-stump.

With that the tall, blond spinner roared into the outfield like a lighthouse ablaze and on the hoof with his teammates in giddy pursuit. And why not. Harmer’s career-best 6/16, and the 4/104 he claimed in the first innings, gave him his first 10-wicket haul in Tests.

That sealed South Africa’s 176-run win and the 2-1 series triumph that took them to the top of the world rankings and to second place in the WTC standings.

A crowd of 9,729 stood and applauded. One of them, a boy of maybe 10 in a cap, t-shirt and shorts, leapt the boundary fence, sped to the middle, snatched a stump, and raced all the way back. He tossed his prize into the crowd, but was not able to complete his heist; he was collared by security staff, who handled him with undue roughness and carried him away.

That was ugly. But not this — as South Africa’s players embarked on a lap around the ground to thank the fans, another child sat on a seat and wore a cardboard cutout mask on his face. In 2018 South Africa supporters wore masks fashioned from photographs of the face of Candice Warner, David Warner’s wife, in a cowardly and disgusting attempt to enrage the player.

That kid at Newlands on Saturday lifted his mask and beamed the biggest smile at the world. Then he lowered his mask onto his face again. Suddenly a cardboard cutout of Temba Bavuma’s face was smiling at the world. That’s what progress looks like.

cricket_news.title: Amite Hasan replaces concussed Mominul for second West Indies Test
cricket_news.summary: News   •  West Indies tour of Bangladesh, 2026  Amite Hasan replaces concussed Mominul for second West Indies Test  In the opening Test against West Indies, Jaker Ali Anik was named as Bangladesh's concussion substitute for the rest of the game
cricket_news.content:
Bangladesh have recalled wicketkeeper-batter Amite Hasan for the second Test against West Indies, scheduled to begin in Sylhet from November 5.

Cricbuzz earlier reported that Mominul Haque was doubtful for the second Test. Bangladesh Cricket Board announced that the left-handed batter will be replaced by Amite.

Amite, the right-handed batter with plenty of domestic runs under his belt, has played only one Test so far, against Zimbabwe in Harare earlier this year. He managed scores of 4 & 25.

“Right-hander Amite Hasan has replaced Mominul Haque, who is unavailable for the second Test due to the concussion rule that states that a player diagnosed with a concussion must observe a mandatory minimum of seven calendar days away from play before returning to the field,” BCB said in a statement.

In the opening Test against West Indies, Jaker Ali Anik was named as Bangladesh's concussion substitute for the rest of the game, after Mominul showed signs of concussion following a blow to the head.

Mominul was hurt while fielding in the 78th over of West Indies' first innings on the third day, when he dropped Roston Chase on 27 while fielding at short leg. Later, team management officials informed that he will not take any further part in the match.

Bangladesh are trailing by 1-0 in the ongoing two-match Test series against West Indies, which is part of the ICC World Test Championship. The visitors earned an eight-wicket win over them inside four days in the opening Test at Dhaka.

cricket_news.title: Rabada, Harmer bowl South Africa to series win and No. 1 ranking
cricket_news.summary: Reports   •  Australia tour of South Africa, 2026  Rabada, Harmer bowl South Africa to series win and No. 1 ranking  Australia, chasing 288, were bowled out for 111 to give South Africa a 176-run win in the third Test in Cape Town
cricket_news.content:
All three results were possible when the final day of the series began at Newlands. By Lunch, only one result was on the table. Kagiso Rabada struck twice in the first over and Simon Harmer spun a web with figures of 6 for 16 as Australia, chasing 288, were bowled out for 111 to give South Africa a 176-run win in the third Test. As a result, the hosts also took the series 2-1 and reclaimed the No. 1 Test ranking.

Australia must have begun the day believing they could chase this down. That belief, though, lasted three balls. Rabada, who was down with illness on the second and third days, had Matt Renshaw, the series' leading run-scorer, gloving a ball down the leg side to Ryan Rickelton. Three balls later in the same opening over, he trapped Marnus Labuschagne lbw.

Travis Head, Australia's best hope, hit three fours before Rabada had him caught at gully by Marco Jansen in the seventh over. It was Rabada's 350th Test wicket, and Australia were reeling at 22 for 3 at the time.

Harmer came on in the 12th over and found sharp turn out of the rough straight away. To make things worse, Josh Inglis was run out for four after a needless single to silly point. In the 18th over, Harmer had Alex Carey caught off a reverse sweep, with Marco Jansen diving forward at backward point. Two balls later, Cooper Connolly was caught behind. Mitchell Starc survived 24 balls before popping a catch to short leg off the last ball of the morning session and Australia went to Lunch at 60/7, having lost seven wickets in the morning.

Cameron Green and Pat Cummins then dug in, with 11 successive overs gone without a run. Green, on 27 off 110 balls, finally tried to break the shackles, dancing down to Harmer, and was bowled through the gate. Cummins batted 90 balls for 11 and added 45 for the ninth wicket with Nathan Lyon, who made an unbeaten 33, before Harmer trapped him lbw. Two overs later, Harmer bowled Josh Hazlewood with a ball that drifted in and turned away to hit the top of off, bowling Australia out for 111 in 57.1 overs and bringing up a famous series win for South Africa.

Harmer, who took 21.1 overs to claim his six wickets, 14 of them maidens, became the first South African spinner to take a Test ten-wicket haul at Cape Town. Rabada, who had set off this slide with the new ball, finished with 3 for 39.

The win was set up on the fourth day by Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder, whose centuries and 154-run sixth-wicket stand pulled South Africa out of trouble and gave them a total to defend.

It was Australia's first Test series defeat since March 2023, and only the fourth time they have lost a three-match series after winning the first Test. As a result of them going down, New Zealand claimed the first position on the World Test Championship table, pushing Australia out of the top two for the first time this cycle.

Brief scores: South Africa 329 (Marques Ackerman 95, Marco Jansen 52; Mitchell Starc 6-72) & 387 (Wiaan Mulder 115, Ryan Rickelton 101; Mitchell Starc 3-65) beat Australia 429 (Josh Inglis 102, Alex Carey 80; Simon Harmer 4-104, Marco Jansen 3-60) & 111 (Nathan Lyon 33*; Simon Harmer 6-16, Kagiso Rabada 3-39) by 176 runs.

cricket_news.title: 'We came here to win the series': Chase keeps West Indies focused
cricket_news.summary: News   •  Dhaka Test  'We came here to win the series': Chase keeps West Indies focused  West Indies are looking to seal a series win in Sylhet after taking an early lead in Dhaka, while Bangladesh's hopes of reaching the WTC final have suffered a major setback
cricket_news.content:
West Indies captain Roston Chase said on Saturday that they are eyeing a series win over Bangladesh to end the current ICC World Test Championship (WTC) cycle on a high.

West Indies earned an eight-wicket win over Bangladesh in the opening Test of the two-match series in Dhaka, which is part of the ongoing WTC cycle.

Both teams will now move to Sylhet for the second Test, scheduled to begin on November 5.

The touring skipper said they were not getting carried away after winning the series opener, as the job was still only half done.

"Winning a Test match anywhere in any conditions is a beautiful feeling, but we came here to win the series. This is just the first of two legs," said Chase.

Chase said the bowlers broke the backbone of Bangladesh's batting in the second innings by picking up quick wickets, which set the tone for them in the game.

"I think the start that we had in the second innings with the ball, I thought that we put them under pressure and we got, I think it was four quick wickets early in that second innings," Chase said.

"I thought that really broke the back of the Bangladeshi batting and then we just had to stay patient from there and try to get the other wickets, and that we did.

"I don't want to say we let them off, but I thought especially Nayeem this morning played well for the 50 that he got and he kept us out there longer than we wanted to be. But as I said, we stayed patient and we stuck to our plans and our processes and we got them to a total that we thought was more than manageable," he added.

"I thought 170 was manageable because I thought the wicket was still a good wicket. I didn't think the wicket had any devils in it, it was still playing consistently. I thought it had a bit of bounce as well, probably the first time I saw a wicket in Dhaka with so much bounce," he said.

"I just wanted us to go out there and get a good start and I thought that was the key, and that we did. And then I just wanted my guys to go out there and play with intent. Although Bangladesh have some good spinners and whatnot, I just wanted them to go out there and, if the Bangladeshi spinners are offline, try to punish them," he said.

"Don't let them just settle and bowl and bowl and bowl, because we know when they get into that rhythm and they start spotting the ball in front of you and they start to get that confidence, and then things start to happen. So I just thought that start was very key for us as well," he added.

Chase said they had taken a last-minute decision to leave out Kemar Roach and play spinner Joshua Bishop after the pitch was shaved on the first morning.

"It was shocking for us to see that much grass off," Chase said. "We made a last-minute change in leaving out Roach and bringing in Bishop."

"When the green grass got shaven off, I thought it would be more suitable for the spinners. I thought that we read it correctly," he added.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto said their dream of reaching the World Test Championship final had become difficult after the defeat to West Indies.

A win against West Indies would have put them in a strong position towards their goal of earning a spot in the WTC final, but the defeat has dented their hopes. They now need four wins and a draw from their remaining five Test matches against West Indies, South Africa and England.

"It's difficult, to be very honest. But as I said in the first press conference, we are looking at one match at a time. This Test match we didn't play our best. So looking forward to the second Test, how we come back strongly," said Najmul, while rejecting suggestions that the points table had influenced the preparation of the surface.

"The points table did not come to mind. The condition was set by thinking about the opponent's strengths and weaknesses. I don't think it was made thinking about the Test Championship final," he said.

"Spinners have always won us matches in the past. That confidence was there before and it is still there. I don't think we made too many mistakes about the conditions," he said.

"After setting 170, we believed it could be defended, given the state of the pitch. Unfortunately, that didn't happen. We could have bowled a bit better on this wicket. We didn't bowl very well," he said.

"We could not pick the length very well. It was a bit scattered. In the fourth innings we took only two wickets," he added.

Najmul pointed to his own first-innings batting as a key factor in the defeat, saying he should have taken greater responsibility as a senior batter.

"In the first innings, I should have taken more responsibility as a senior batsman. I have played here for a long time and I know these conditions. If I could have made a big score, the team could have been 370 instead of 270," said Najmul.

"We fell back in the first innings. We knew batting later would be difficult. I would say the mistake was made in the first innings," he said, adding that they also missed Mushfiqur Rahim, who sat out the Test after injuring his finger during preparations for the opening game.

"We missed him. An experienced cricketer in this kind of condition. It would have been good if he was here," Najmul concluded.

cricket_news.title: Yuvraj Singh sees a leader and an ODI batter in Abhishek Sharma
cricket_news.summary: News   •  India cricket  Yuvraj Singh sees a leader and an ODI batter in Abhishek Sharma  The India legend, who introduced Abhishek to golf, believes the opener has the leadership qualities to take on greater responsibility and deserves a place in the ODI squad
cricket_news.content:
Whether golf can really help a cricketer's batting skills is a matter of interpretation, particularly because the ball is stationary in the game of greens and fairways, while it is necessarily in motion in the game of bat and ball. That said, cricketers are known to possess the hand-eye coordination that golf also demands, and the sport could further augment that skill, apart from helping in swing movement, power-hitting, ball sense and competitive drive. Abhishek Sharma may be a classic example.

Cricketers are known to take to golf like a fish to water, more so overseas players than Indians, but Abhishek has already developed a liking for the sport. He is often spotted on the fairways with his guru, Yuvraj Singh, who, it is said, introduced his disciple to the game during the Covid pandemic. Abhishek has since taken to golf seriously and is often seen at golf courses of Chandigarh and New Delhi with Yuvraj.

Both also strolled on the green expanses even in exotic cities and locations. Earlier this summer, they went to play a few rounds during visits to Sardinia, an island in Italy, and Marrakech, in Morocco, before that. So taken is Abhishek with swinging his club around that he would even play the golf regularly during the IPL, joining his overseas teammates, who rarely miss an opportunity to hit the course, whether in Hyderabad or at other IPL venues where SRH play their away games.

His golfing skills may well be reflected in his batting — in his huge bat swing, power-hitting and timing. With experience, he is also committing fewer mistakes and often gets the ball to attain both altitude and distance, a skill that golfers often seek to develop through the swing of the club: both height and distance.

“Golf helps with the bat swing and head position a lot. The top hand, which in Abhishek’s case is the left, gets extended, and that helps with the swing. It also helps with temperament. In golf, you tend to make mistakes, but you also learn to make course corrections. So it can help minimise mistakes and build concentration, which should come in handy in cricket too,” says Kiran More, a habitual golfer, explaining how the sport could be helping Abhishek.

“I have introduced him to golf so that he can unwind from cricket,” says Yuvraj Singh, an avid golfer himself, of course. But Yuvraj, who was in Mumbai for a promotional event on Friday, addressed the two elephants in the room — when and whether Abhishek would be ready for the ODIs and whether he was prepared to take on a leadership role.

Abhishek is being particularly credited with mentoring Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the teenager who is yet to cement his place in the national side despite his abundance of talent. The chemistry between Abhishek and Sooryavanshi, on display during the third T20I against New Zealand in Wellington recently, made for a pleasing sight.

The two put on 133 for the first wicket in 7.1 overs with Abhishek hammering a breathtaking century and Sooryavanshi hammering a typically belligerent 45 off 19 balls. There was no sign of insecurity in Abhishek in the way he treated and encouraged Sooryavanshi. On another occasion, it was Abhishek, who was first to comfort Sooryavanshi after he had missed a century (97 off 29 balls) in the IPL Eliminator earlier this year even though his own franchise was at the receiving end of his sensational batting.

“Well, it’s too early to say whether he has the makings of a captain, but I feel he has all the qualities of a leader. I think he encourages the younger guys in state cricket as well. I love the way he encourages Sooryavanshi, puts his hand on his shoulder and motivates him. I think that’s a good sign of a senior leader, whatever you want to call it,” Yuvraj tells Cricbuzz.

“If you want to captain India one day, I think it’s important to captain your IPL side. That gives you the kind of confidence you need to lead India. I’m sure time will tell whether he is capable of doing it. If it’s in his destiny, I’m sure he’ll get the opportunity. If not, then so be it. But I’m sure he’ll finish as a great white-ball player, whether he becomes captain or not.”

Yuvraj also called for Abhishek’s inclusion in the ODI set-up, something one understands, even India head coach Gautam Gambhir wants. “Whether he has scored 35, 100 or 31, 100, the point is that he has been performing consistently in white-ball cricket for a very long time. What more he needs to do to get into the ODI squad, I don't know. Maybe he needs to contribute more with his bowling and fielding. But that will only happen if he gets an opportunity to play.

“There are always areas to improve, and I think unless you give a player a chance, where is he going to showcase his talent? I understand that the situation is difficult right now because there is so much competition for places in the squad, along with some big names. But look at Sooryavanshi. He was brilliant and made his own place in the T20 squad. If you feel that Abhishek is performing brilliantly at the moment, then somewhere you have to make a place for him to play 50-over cricket until the World Cup.”

cricket_news.title: India seek bowling solutions in bid for 4-1 finish
cricket_news.summary: Previews   •  India tour of New Zealand, 2026  India seek bowling solutions in bid for 4-1 finish  India have secured the series but their bowling numbers since the T20 World Cup remain a concern heading into the final game against a resurgent New Zealand
cricket_news.content:
No time to rest. With just one intervening day before the switch from Eden Park to Seddon Park, the final T20I of the series (and India’s 40th of the year) turns into a short stopover. The attention has already started drifting towards the one-dayers, especially since India’s decorated batting duo has landed on the same island for the 50-over challenge.

India have pocketed the T20I series, but the manner of their 87-run defeat in Auckland was a reminder that New Zealand haven’t exactly been blanked out, but outmuscled in a series deep-fried in runs.

Shreyas Iyer called the defeat a “great learning curve,” conceding that Eden Park’s unique dimensions posed a fresh challenge for many within the team. The home team fared better on the ground with a short straight boundary, extra bounce, and strong winds that prevented dew, powering to 259 and handing India their second-heaviest run-defeat ever.

India wouldn’t have minded the hiccup: the series has allowed them to test out combinations, move things around slightly, and find new batting heroes. But the bowling, particularly in the second half, has been a cause of worry. Among Full-Member sides, India have the worst average and second-worst economy since the T20 World Cup this year.

New Zealand have been served greatly by an in-form Glenn Phillips, who has been exceptional at shifting gears, and found support in Daryl Mitchell, Bevon Jacobs and Michael Bracewell. Mitchell Santner has been the standout bowler across both teams, while Jacob Duffy came back strongly after leaking runs in two games. They’ve managed to put India’s batting under pressure twice, and it came by restricting them in the Powerplay. That could be the defining factor in the final game as well. As could be their catching: New Zealand have dropped as many as 12 this series.

When: India vs New Zealand, 5th T20I, November 1, 2026, 12:30 PM IST, 8:00 PM Local time

What to expect: Compared to Auckland, it gets cooler in Hamilton, with temperatures dropping to as low as 4 °C early morning. It’s likely to hover between 12-15 °C during match times. The winds, though, might not be as big a factor. Seddon Park has usually been a high-scoring venue, and the run-fest is likely to continue.

New Zealand: The hosts have changed around their pace attack as well, some of which have been forced. Lockie Ferguson and Matt Henry are injured, and Kyle Jamieson will re-link with them in the ODIs. It’s given a surprise chance to Matthew Fisher, and the quick has taken three wickets in his two appearances so far. Now that they’ve broken the losing streak, they might consider sticking with the same combination.

Predicted XI: Tim Seifert (wk), Finn Allen, Daryl Mitchell, Glenn Phillips, Bevon Jacobs, Michael Bracewell, Mitchell Santner (c), Nathan Smith, Adam Milne, Jacob Duffy, Matthew Fisher

India: Ishan Kishan, who had been ruled out of the second and third T20I, returned in the fourth, also taking up wicketkeeping duties. It remains to be seen whether Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, swapped in and out for those two games, gets a chance in the dead rubber, especially if Sanju Samson isn’t taking the gloves.

A pace-heavy lineup hasn’t afforded space for Kuldeep Yadav and Varun Chakaravarthy yet, despite Axar Patel’s poor returns. All four quicks have been given sufficient game time around Arshdeep Singh’s fixed spot. They could go back to Bhuvneshwar Kumar, whose much-awaited comeback has produced only one wicket in three games.

Predicted XI: Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson/Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Ishan Kishan (wk), Shreyas Iyer (c), Tilak Varma, Axar Patel, Nitish Kumar Reddy/Shivam Dube, Naman Dhir, Arshdeep Singh, Prince Yadav/Bhuvneshwar Kumar, Mayank Yadav

- India have conceded 200+ 11 times in 39 matches, the most by a team in a calendar year across all T20 cricket

- Glenn Phillips now has more runs (276) than anyone against India in a T20I series

- New Zealand’s catching success this year stands at 74.1 per cent, the second-worst among the top-12 ranked T20I teams in the world, after Pakistan (73.1)

"You need a ton of runs to even have a sniff of beating India, so for us to be able to put that sort of score on the board today (259), I guess it'll give us confidence going forward. It's our first time being up in that 250 range, at least in the time that I can remember. I don't think you've ever got enough to feel comfortable with this side." – New Zealand batter Glenn Phillips after the 4th T20I.

“Some phenomenal shots, which were like pure bliss. Kudos to him. He's been consistent throughout the series, so a lot to learn from him,” India captain Shreyas Iyer, on Phillips’s knock in the 4th T20I.

cricket_news.title: Bangladesh's spin gamble raises questions after Mirpur defeat
cricket_news.summary: News   •  West Indies tour of Bangladesh, 2026  Bangladesh's spin gamble raises questions after Mirpur defeat  With the West Indian spinners extracting more turn and out-bowling the hosts, it leaves Bangladesh with plenty to ponder over ahead of the Sylhet Test
cricket_news.content:
Did Bangladesh pay the price of preparing a spinning deck? It was a question that came up for discussion after the hosts’ eight-wicket loss to West Indies in the first Test at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium on Saturday (October 31).

While Bangladesh looked to take a significant step towards their dream of playing in the ICC World Test Championship final with a ploy of outfoxing West Indies with a spin-heavy attack, it hardly paid any dividends as the tourists emerged better placed for the strategy.

West Indies’ spinners dominated the Test, with left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican taking nine wickets, which included a five-wicket haul in the first innings. Captain Roston Chase took five wickets in the second innings with his off-spin to set up the match for his side before the batters got the job done.

The spinners from the two sides brought different bowling approaches. But what was more surprising was the fact that the West Indian spinners extracted a greater average turn - 3.5 degrees - compared to Bangladesh’s 3 degrees.

“I don't know why we have forgotten to turn the ball. If we cannot turn the ball on this wicket I am not sure where we will turn the ball,” a member of the national team management told Cricbuzz on the request of anonymity, after the Mirpur Test.

“I am not sure whether it is a technical thing or something else because these same bowlers managed to turn the ball better on flatter wickets.

“I think our bowlers tried to ball with more pace while the West Indians bowled a lot slower and that probably allowed them to turn the ball more than us,” he added.

There are also arguments over the Bangladesh spinners’ mindset and whether it presents them as attacking options.

“It's fair to say we are not traditionally attacking spinners as we believe that if we can stop the flow of the runs, pressure will mount on the opponents and most of our spinners play cricket carrying that philosophy," the aforementioned team management member said.

“We hardly have a plan B and you cannot ask them to change their approach right in the middle of the game. But the time has come for us to start having a plan B so that if needed, we can attack. And by that I mean having the courage to buy wickets.

“You can argue whether with such a small total [to defend] whether that would have been a good approach or not. But at the same time you cannot defend such a total with a mindset of not leaking runs,” he added.

Quite a few eyebrows were raised after Bangladesh opted for a spin-friendly wicket in Mirpur, considering that the strategy has resulted in more losses than wins in Tests in recent times. Moreover, Bangladesh’s fast bowlers have started to make a name for themselves through their recent performances and there is a feeling that not backing them to come good was not wise.

The absence of pace bowler Nahid Rana, who is ruled out of the series due to injury, would have played a part in making such a decision. But with the spinners unable to turn the ball as much as their opponents on a track tailor-made for them raises questions over the decision taken up by the team management.

Whether earning points in the WTC was a major reason behind this decision is a matter of discussion. But as they go back to the drawing board ahead of the second Test in Sylhet from November 5, Bangladesh have plenty to think about having endured successive defeats after their famous win against Australia in Darwin.

cricket_news.title: Jansen's long night of the soul dawns bright
cricket_news.summary: News   •  Australia tour of South Africa, 2026  Jansen's long night of the soul dawns bright  The South African allrounder capped a prolific series with a Player of the Series award after helping his side overturn a first-Test defeat
cricket_news.content:
Marco Jansen had one of those nights on Friday, a knotty, thorny sequence of long, dark hours when he goes “cuckoo in the head”, as he had told a press conference on Wednesday.

Back behind the microphones on Saturday, Jansen said: “I probably slept one-and-a-half hours, maybe two. That’s because of looking out my window, going to the bathroom, having a coke. I hardly got any sleep, thinking of what we could do, what I could do, what’s going to be required, what if things don’t go our way …”

Things did go South Africa’s way at Newlands on Saturday. Australia, who chased a target of 288, were bowled out for 111. That earned the home side the series 2-1 and put them on top of the ICC Test rankings for the first time since January 2016. It also hiked South Africa — the WTC champions — into second place in those standings. The Aussies, who started the series on top of the rankings and second in the standings, are now second and third. How did that feel?

“When we end up on the right side of things, for a split second there’s a sigh of relief that it’s over,” Jansen said. “But after that there’s a really good and excited and pumped feeling, knowing that if I played well I’ve contributed. And also if I didn’t play well I still contributed, whether it was on the field or off the field.

“This is a team thing. It’s not an individual thing, and that gives me a lot of joy and happiness. It makes it very much worth it.”

Jansen contributed directly in the first innings at Newlands, hitting seven fours in his 52 and taking 3/60 in the first innings. His second innings might have been what kept him awake on Friday night: he was bounced out by Mitchell Starc for an eight-ball duck. On Saturday he bowled eight wicketless overs for 17.

But he was named player of the series. That's what happens when you bring your team back into the rubber with a 100-ball 85 after they’ve slumped to 110/6. And then take 5/33. Jansen did that in the second Test at St George’s Park, where South Africa found a way to win by an innings and 31 runs after most of the first two days’ play was lost to rain and a wet outfield. And, on top of that, under the pressure of having lost the first Test at Kingsmead by 214 runs. Despite the size of those margins the series produced intensely competitive cricket.

“It wasn’t easy,” Jansen said. “There were a lot of ups and downs; ebbs and flows. It was never a case of one team having the upper hand for an extended period of time. There was a stage where I was sitting in the [Newlands] changeroom and you think, ‘Yes! We’re in this thing!’ And then four wickets fall and I’m like, ‘What the hell are we doing?!’”

Jansen’s exploits in the series have made him Test cricket’s top-ranked bowler and allrounder. Did that make him think of himself as special?

“No. I just see myself as a lightie [youngster] from Klerksdorp. When I started playing professionally and started my career for the Proteas I never thought of getting into the top 10 bowling or allrounder rankings. Fast forward to now where I’m on top of those lists; firstly it’s surreal and secondly, like my dad used to tell myself and my brother [Duan], ‘Moenie dat jou kop te groot raak nie [don’t let you head get too big]. I remind myself where I come from and what I’ve had to be to be consistent and perform consistently.”

Maybe Jansen’s most valuable asset is that he has maintained the link between his smalltown former life and the big time he has reached.

“How old am I now? Twenty-six? [Correct]. Eight years ago I was in high school, and I was watching these guys on TV doing their thing. Now I’m in Cape Town, where a lot of people are watching us.

“I’m better prepared mentally if things don’t go our way, or if we’re doing well, or if I’m batting or bowling well, to stay calm and composed. To handle those situations better is the difference.”

Jansen can afford to be more inwardly focused than Temba Bavuma, who has to answer not only for himself but also for the team he captains. Happily for all concerned Bavuma is good at that.

“In a weird way, but also a beautiful way, we are driven by this ambition to achieve what it is that we want to achieve; the narratives and the sentiments and the stories that are created around it all,” Bavuma told a press conference.

“You have to answer questions why a certain guy is playing. But we stick to what we want to achieve, and we’ve surpassed a lot of those things. Did I think two or two-and-a-half years ago that we’d be in this position? Probably not.”

Key to that happening is Shukri Conrad, South Africa’s imaginative, maverick coach. How he and Bavuma, who comes across as measured and logical, get along is a fascinating study in contrasts. But, clearly, they do.

“Shuks uses a crazy formula. I keep questioning him to make sure we’re making the right decision. But, whatever decision we make, we back it with 100% conviction.”

Bavuma called the series, in which all three matches went to five days, “an enthralling 15 days of cricket”. He also labelled it “15 days of pressure”.

Now that the pressure’s off here’s hoping Bavuma, and Jansen, sleep well on Saturday.

cricket_news.title: Zaman, Minhas and Baig power Pakistan's tri-series triumph
cricket_news.summary: Reports   •  ODI tri-series, 2026   Zaman, Minhas and Baig power Pakistan's tri-series triumph  The Pakistan trio trumped Kamindu Mendis' century as they chased down Sri Lanka's 325/8 with three wickets to spare
cricket_news.content:
Fakhar Zaman's century trumped Kamindu Mendis' ton as Pakistan secured a three-wicket win in the final against Sri Lanka in Lahore to clinch the tri-series. Mendis' 131 and Pavan Rathnayake's 77 were instrumental in Sri Lanka posting 325 for 8. Pakistan's chase was powered by Zaman's 127, along with important contributions from Saad Baig (74) and Arafat Minhas (31-ball 61) as the hosts overhauled the target with 1.3 overs to spare.

Sri Lanka made a steady start after being asked to bat, with Avishka Fernando and Kamindu Mendis negotiating the new ball before gradually shifting gears. Fernando struck two fours and a six off Naseem Shah in the sixth over to inject some momentum while Kamindu hit a maximum off Shaheen Afridi in the 10th over, taking Sri Lanka to 51 for 0. Kamindu was given out caught behind off Arafat Minhas but successfully overturned the decision on review. Pakistan, meanwhile, bowled some tight overs, including a maiden from Haris Rauf to Fernando in the 17th, before Salman Agha capitalised in the next, trapping Fernando lbw for 38.

Kamindu ended a boundary drought and went past fifty while Kusal Mendis launched Rauf for a six. But Agha produced a moment of brilliance to dismiss Kusal, taking a sharp return catch to leave Sri Lanka at 109/2 in the 22nd over. Pakistan had an opportunity to put the brakes on the innings, but Kamindu and Pavan Rathnayake ensured Sri Lanka made good progress. The pair put on a century stand, the scoring rate picked up, and milestones followed as Kamindu reached his maiden ODI century while Rathnayake brought up his fourth 50-plus score in the series, taking Sri Lanka past 250 in the 41st over.

The third-wicket pair added 146 before the partnership ended when Kamindu was trapped lbw by Afridi. Dasun Shanaka smashed a six and two fours in a quickfire 17 off nine balls before Afridi dismissed him, while Rauf accounted for Rathnayake and Naseem sent Janith Liyanage back, as Sri Lanka lost five wickets for just 29 runs. However, Sahan Arachchige and Maheesh Theekshana added some useful runs towards the end to help Sri Lanka set a challenging target for Pakistan.

Pakistan's chase began with a couple of setbacks as Dilshan Madushanka bagged the wickets of Maaz Sadaqat and Babar Azam in his first two overs. Fakhar Zaman and Saad Baig ensured that the innings did not stagnate in their bid to consolidate. Zaman struck maximums wile Baig dealt in regular boundaries, taking Pakistan to 50 for 2 after 10 overs. The pair maintained a steady scoring rate, with Baig bringing up his maiden ODI fifty and Zaman crossing fifty as well, with the century partnership sandwiched between the milestones.

Pakistan crossed 150 in the 26th over before the 149-run third wicket stand came to an end when Baig handed a catch back to Theekshana to depart for 74 off 75, with 11 fours in his outing. Zaman, meanwhile, continued unperturbed as he brought up his 12th ODI hundred and cleared the fence regularly. He was eventually bowled by Madushanka, with his 99-ball knock including six sixes and 11 fours. Salman Agha followed a short while later, bowled by Dunith Wellalage, leaving Pakistan needing 96 off the last 13 overs, which became 82 off the last 10 overs.

Pakistan went through a dry spell, without any boundary, for 10 overs before Arafat Minhas struck a four off Shanaka in the 43rd over, and another boundary off Asitha Fernando in the 45th. Hasan Nawaz's scoring was on the slower side but he supported Minhas in building a partnership as they brought the equation to 46 off the last five overs. A couple of good overs for Pakistan, which included sixes for Minhas off Shanaka and Madushanka, made it 18 off 18. Minhas brought up a 28-ball fifty with a six off Fernando, followed by another maximum and a four before he was eventually dismissed. Faheem Ashraf fell in the same over but Pakistan got over the line when Afridi struck a six off Madushanka in the penultimate over.

Brief scores: Sri Lanka 325/8 in 50 overs (Kamindu Mendis 131, Pavan Rathnayake 77; Shaheen Afridi 2-50) lost to Pakistan 331/7 in 48.3 overs (Fakhar Zaman 127, Saad Baig 74, Arafat Minhas 61; Dilshan Madushanka 3-63) by 3 wickets.

cricket_news.title: WTC scenarios: South Africa replace Australia in top-two after Cape Town Test
cricket_news.summary: Statistics & Analysis   •  World Test Championship  WTC scenarios: South Africa replace Australia in top-two after Cape Town Test  Holders South Africa climb up to second while New Zealand are at the top of the pile
cricket_news.content:
South Africa’s series win over Australia and West Indies’ win over Bangladesh in Dhaka have widened the gap between the top three and the bottom six teams. New Zealand have surged to the top of the WTC table after Australia’s defeat, pushing the Aussies out of the top two. South Africa jumped to the second position - after a Cape Town win - with a points percentage (PCT) of 71.43 in the 2025-27 cycle.

With 10 Test series among nine teams still to go in this current WTC cycle, no team has booked its place in the final yet. Here are the qualification scenarios for all the teams:

Note: In the WTC 2025-2027, teams will get 12 points for a win, 4 for a draw, and 6 for a tie. The points percentage system (PCT) will be used to determine the leaderboard. PCT = Points won by a team / Points contested * 100.

Remaining fixtures:  IND (2 Tests, home), AUS (4 Tests, away), SL (2 Tests, home), PAK (2 Tests, away)

New Zealand have climbed to the top of the WTC table after Australia’s defeat in Cape Town with 72.22 PCT. They still have 10 Tests to play in this cycle. Of the remaining 120 points, if they win 6 Tests, they will finish on 64.6, which might not be enough. While seven wins and three losses would take them to 70.83%, then they will have a strong chance for a top-two finish. They have four home fixtures against India and Sri Lanka, which will decide their fate for a second WTC final appearance.

Remaining fixtures:  BAN (2 Tests, home), ENG (3 Tests, home), SL (2 Tests, away)

Series win over Australia has put South Africa in a strong position for a top-two finish. They have seven games remaining in this cycle and five of them at home. If they win the series against Bangladesh and England by clean sweeps, it could take Bavuma’s side past 71.42%, which will be sufficient for a ticket to the final. Four wins will take Proteas to 64.28 PCT, which might not be sufficient.

Remaining fixtures:  NZ (4 Tests, home), IND (5 Tests, away)

Before the South Africa tour, Australia were on top of the table with 80 PCT, with eight wins and just two defeats from ten matches. But two successive losses put them out of the top two for the first time in this cycle. Still, they have their fate in their hands. They currently have 69.23 points percentage, but face tough tests against New Zealand at home and against India in the Border-Gavaskar Trophy in early 2027. They need to win at least six out of their nine remaining Tests to take them to 67.2%. If they win only four and play out a couple of draws with a split of results, it will likely enough to keep them in the top two.

Remaining fixtures: NZ (2 Tests, away); Aus (5 Tests, home)

India sit fourth on 51.52 PCT after the Colombo draw. Winning all their remaining seven Tests, will give them a PCT of 70.37. Even six wins, will take them to 65%. If they win five Tests and play out a draw, then they will need other results to go their way. A 0-2 loss in New Zealand followed by a 5-0 home sweep of Australia would leave India on 59.26%, which might not be sufficient to finish in the top two.

Remaining fixtures: WI (1 Test, home), SA (2 Tests, away), ENG (2 Tests, home)

A defeat in Dhaka against West Indies puts Bangladesh behind India at fifth position with 47.62%. Now they need to win all their five remaining matches to go past the 65% mark. If they lose even one more Test, it will take them to only 61.11%, which will not be enough for them to reach the top two finish.

Remaining fixtures:  PAK (2 Tests, away), NZ (2 Tests, away), SA (2 Tests, home)

Currently,  Sri Lanka have only 33.33 PCT from six matches they have played so far. A draw against India in their home Test keeps their WTC final dream alive. With six Tests left, winning all of them would take them to 66.67, which might be sufficient for their qualification chances if other results go their way.
